sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Power load forecasting is a core component in the operation and planning of power
systems, playing a critical role in ensuring the safe and stable operation of the grid, improv-
ing energy efficiency, and optimizing resource allocation. It is not only a key method for
achieving power supply and demand balance but also a vital foundation for supporting
the economy, safety, and sustainability of the power system [ 1–3]. With the continuous
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 https://doi.org/10.3390/app15052435
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 2 of 24
expansion of modern power systems, increasing complexity, and the ongoing develop-
ment of intelligence, the importance of load forecasting has become more prominent. This
is especially true in the context of large-scale integration of renewable energy sources
and the accelerated reform of electricity markets, where the operational environment of
power systems is facing unprecedented challenges and uncertainties. Short-term load
forecasting (such as hourly to weekly forecasting), as a fundamental element for power
system scheduling and energy efficiency management, plays a crucial role in all stages
of grid operation. It is widely used in areas such as demand-side management, energy
storage system optimization, grid regulation strategy development, and power generation
planning [4–6]. High-precision load forecasting not only helps power companies optimize
operational scheduling, allocate power generation resources efficiently, and reduce energy
losses, but also effectively lowers grid operating costs and enhances economic benefits.
At the same time, accurate forecasting helps to address potential load fluctuations and
unexpected situations in grid operations, ensuring the safety and reliability of the grid and
providing strong support for the stable operation of the power system [ 7–9]. However,
power load data are influenced by various complex factors, including climate change,
economic development, policy adjustments, and fluctuations in user behavior, leading to
significant non-linearity, randomness, and complex temporal characteristics. This makes
traditional statistical methods and linear models limited when it comes to addressing
complex load features, and their prediction accuracy is insufficient to meet the needs of
modern power systems. In particular, with the increasing proportion of renewable energy,
the intermittent and random characteristics of wind and solar power further increase the
difficulty of load forecasting [10–12]. Therefore, leveraging advanced artificial intelligence
technologies and deep learning models to fully mine the potential patterns within power
load data and improve forecasting accuracy has become a key focus of current research.
In previous research on power load forecasting, traditional forecasting methods domi-
nated the field. These methods typically include regression analysis [13], time series models
[14], and gray prediction models [ 15]. Yang et al. [ 16] proposed a comprehensive prob-
abilistic density forecasting method—Gaussian process quantile regression—which can
systematically handle uncertainty in power load data and achieve statistical modeling of
the probability distribution of power load data. Saber et al. [17] proposed a short-term load
forecasting method based on multivariate linear regression (MLR), which improves linear
regression for scenarios with a small number of variables in large datasets and applies
multi-core parallel processing techniques to handle unlimited amounts of historical big
data and forecasting scenarios within an acceptable execution time. Zhao et al. [ 15] pro-
posed a hybrid gray prediction model combining the Ant Lion Optimization algorithm and
rolling mechanism, significantly improving the accuracy and reliability of annual power
load forecasting. Velasco et al. [18] proposed a hybrid forecasting method by combining
ARIMA and ANN models, effectively addressing the linear and nonlinear characteristics of
power load data and achieving high-accuracy daily load forecasting. Although traditional
load forecasting methods have been able to meet the needs of early-stage predictions to
a certain extent, with the increasing complexity of power systems, these methods have
gradually revealed limitations in handling highly nonlinear and dynamic characteristics.
In recent years, data-driven analytical methods, such as phase space reconstruction and
compressed sensing, have been widely applied to address these challenges. Phase space
reconstruction, by uncovering the intrinsic dynamic structures within time series data, can
effectively capture the nonlinear and complex dynamic characteristics of power systems,
thereby being applied to the classification and prediction of transient phenomena in power
grids. Stanescu et al. [ 19] utilized the phase space domain to detect and characterize
these transient phenomena in power grids. Akash et al. [ 20] proposed an efficient method
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 3 of 24
for processing and classifying early discharge signals in transformers by combining com-
pressed sensing technology with machine learning classifiers (such as LSTM), providing
innovative solutions for signal processing and fault detection in power system engineer-
ing. Compressed sensing technology, by extracting key features from a small amount of
data, can maintain high prediction accuracy while reducing the demand for data volume
and computational resources. When combined with machine learning classifiers, these
methods have demonstrated significant advantages in power grid load forecasting and
transient event identification. Therefore, future research could consider integrating these
data-driven technologies into load forecasting models to overcome the limitations of tradi-
tional methods in handling nonlinear and dynamic characteristics. In recent years, with the
rapid development of science and technology and continuous innovation in forecasting
techniques, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in load forecasting has gradually
become a research hotspot. AI technologies, with their powerful data processing capabili-
ties and pattern recognition abilities, have significantly outperformed traditional methods
in terms of prediction accuracy, opening up new directions for power load forecasting.
Among these, neural network methods [ 21,22], due to their strong non-linear mapping
capabilities and self-learning characteristics, have been widely applied; fuzzy logic methods
[23,24], by handling uncertainty and fuzziness, have provided effective tools for modeling
complex load variations; and support vector machine methods [25,26], with their excellent
adaptability to small samples and high-dimensional data, have demonstrated outstanding
performance in load forecasting. It is worth noting that AI methods not only surpass tradi-
tional methods in terms of prediction accuracy but also significantly enhance the ability
to uncover hidden patterns in load data, especially when it comes to handling complex
temporal characteristics, multi-dimensional input variables, and non-linear relationships.
The rapid development of these technologies has provided strong support for addressing
the diversity and uncertainty of power systems, while also promoting the shift in power
load forecasting from an experience-driven approach to a data-driven paradigm.
In contemporary research, many scholars have explored the application of artificial
intelligence (AI) in power load forecasting to address the challenges posed by complex and
dynamic forecasting environments [27,28]. Li et al. [29] proposed a short-term load forecast-
ing method based on deep learning (DLSF), which converts numerical forecasting problems
into image processing tasks and combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and
multi-layer neural networks to effectively improve the accuracy and efficiency of power
load forecasting. However, CNN lacks the ability to capture long-term dependencies when

sections.title: 1 A comprehensive load forecasting model combining CNN, LSTM, Multi-Head Self-
sections.text:
Attention (MHSA), Global Attention Mechanism (GAM), and Channel Attention
Mechanism (CAM) is proposed. By integrating multiple deep learning techniques,
this model fully explores the complex spatial features and temporal dependencies
of power grid load data, effectively enhancing the model’s forecasting accuracy and
adaptability. An end-to-end efficient forecasting framework is designed, integrating
the entire process from high-dimensional feature extraction to time series modeling,
and attention optimization. This framework builds a seamless load forecasting system
from input to output, ensuring the model’s efficiency and practicality.

sections.title: 2 We innovatively introduce multi-head self-attention, global attention mechanism,
sections.text:
and channel attention mechanism: The multi-head self-attention mechanism is used
to model the global dependencies of long-sequence data, while the global attention
mechanism enables the model to focus more specifically on important temporal
features. The channel attention mechanism weights and optimizes different feature
channels, highlighting important information and reducing redundant interference,
significantly enhancing the model’s feature extraction capability.
3. Experimental validation of the model’s superiority: Through experiments on three
real-world power grid load datasets, it is demonstrated that the model proposed
in this paper outperforms existing mainstream methods in multiple key metrics,
including forecasting accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency, providing
reliable support for the optimized scheduling and load management of smart grids.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we provide a brief
review of related work. Section 3 presents the details of the proposed model. In Section 4,
we comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed model through experiments.
Finally, Section 5 summarizes the work conducted in this paper.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.text:
Electric load forecasting is a critical component of energy management, significantly
impacting the efficiency and reliability of power systems. With the rapid development
of smart grids, the demand for accurate load forecasting has grown at an increasing rate,
driving continuous innovation and advancement in related models and methods. In recent
years, research has focused on deep learning models, federated learning approaches, and
the integration of various hybrid models, providing new ideas and tools to enhance the
accuracy and applicability of load forecasting. Supported by a variety of forecasting models
and methods, significant progress has been made in electric load forecasting, including
traditional forecasting methods and artificial intelligence-based forecasting methods, as
well as hybrid forecasting models, which have been proposed in recent years.
Single artificial intelligence forecasting methods, such as CNNs and LSTMs, often
exhibit certain limitations in power grid load forecasting. Due to their fixed model struc-
tures, these methods may only perform well on specific types of load data and poorly
predict complex, nonlinear load data. Additionally, single models are more susceptible
to data noise and outliers, leading to unstable forecasting results and overfitting risks,
particularly when training data are limited or data features are complex. In contrast, hybrid
forecasting models combine multiple different forecasting methods or algorithms, integrat-
ing the advantages of each model to reduce biases and errors from single models, thereby
significantly improving forecasting accuracy and robustness. Hybrid models are better
suited to different types of input data and effectively consider the impact of various factors
on power grid load, providing more comprehensive and reliable forecasting results. Li et al.
[35] proposed a short-term load forecasting method based on a combination of multivariate
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 6 of 24
linear regression and LSTMs, which can accurately predict load behavior, capturing both
global trends and local details. Lv et al. [ 36] proposed a novel hybrid model combining
Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) and LSTMs, which decomposes complex power
load data into components with different frequencies using VMD and then uses LSTMs to
forecast low-frequency and high-frequency components separately, further improving fore-
casting accuracy and robustness. Sekhar et al. [37] combined Bidirectional Long Short-Term
Memory (BiLSTM), Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), and Grey Wolf Optimization
(GWO) to propose a new optimal hybrid strategy for accurate power load forecasting. Luo
et al. [38] proposed a stacking ensemble algorithm for short-term power load forecasting
based on Convolutional Neural Networks–Bidirectional LSTM–Attention and Extreme
Gradient Boosting Trees (XGBoost). This method first uses the Adaptive Hierarchical
Clustering (AHC) algorithm to select datasets with similar daily features, then combines
influencing factors and uses the CNN–BiLSTM–Attention and XGBoost stacking ensemble
algorithm for short-term load forecasting, significantly improving forecasting accuracy. It
is evident that hybrid forecasting models are the mainstream approach used for power grid
load forecasting. However, despite some studies exploring the combination of different
deep learning models, integrating these models with attention mechanisms remains an area
in need of further exploration. The proposed method effectively addresses the limitations
identified in other studies by integrating a multi-modal attention mechanism with a CNN-
LSTM network. The method extracts local spatial features through the CNN module and
captures temporal dependencies using the LSTM layer, achieving dual extraction of spatial
and temporal features. Compared to hybrid models that solely rely on LSTM or CNN,
this approach can more comprehensively capture the complex characteristics of load data.
The introduction of multi-head self-attention and global attention mechanisms enables the
model to dynamically adjust the importance of different time steps and features, thereby
better handling long-range dependencies and complex nonlinear data. In contrast, some
hybrid models (e.g., those based on VMD decomposition) can decompose data but lack the
ability to dynamically weight temporal features. By reweighting feature channels through
the SE module, the proposed method can identify and enhance the feature channels most
relevant to the prediction task while suppressing redundant information. This mechanism
further improves the model’s noise resistance and generalization performance, particularly
excelling in scenarios with high data noise or complex features. The proposed method inte-
grates spatial feature extraction, temporal sequence modeling, and attention mechanisms
into an end-to-end framework, avoiding potential information loss between modules that
may occur in traditional hybrid models. For example, while the method proposed by Li
et al. [35], which combines multivariate linear regression with LSTM, can capture global
trends and local details, the linear regression component may not fully adapt to highly
nonlinear load data. Additionally, through multi-level feature processing and dynamic
attention mechanisms, the proposed method can better adapt to different types of input
data and maintain high prediction accuracy even with limited training data or complex
data features. In contrast, some hybrid models (e.g., those based on BiLSTM-CNN-GWO)
may face overfitting risks when dealing with small-sample data or complex nonlinear
data, despite optimizing the model structure. In summary, by integrating spatial feature
extraction, temporal sequence modeling, and multiple attention mechanisms, the proposed
method not only inherits the advantages of hybrid models but also further optimizes
feature extraction, dynamic weighting, and noise resistance, demonstrating significant
improvements in adaptability, generalization capability, and prediction accuracy, thereby
addressing the limitations present in existing hybrid models.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.text:
This section establishes a CNN-LSTM network based on a multi-modal attention
mechanism for accurate power grid load forecasting, combining the advantages of Con-
volutional Neural Networks (CNNs), Long Short-Term Memory Networks (LSTMs), and
various attention mechanisms. The model’s structure is shown in Figure 1. First, the input
data are processed by the CNN module, where the convolutional layers are used to extract
local features and capture the spatial dependencies of the data. The pooling layers reduce
the dimensionality of the features, lowering the computational complexity while retaining
key features. Next, the features pass through the multi-head self-attention mechanism mod-
ule, which captures long-range dependencies between features through global modeling,
further enhancing the feature representation ability. After extracting spatial features, the
data are input into the LSTM layer to model the dependencies in the time series; here, they
learn the temporal characteristics of load variations. Then, the data pass through the global
attention mechanism module, where the time-series features are weighted, dynamically
adjusting the importance of different time steps, thereby highlighting the time-domain
features that are crucial for load forecasting. Finally, the features pass through the channel
attention module, where the Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) module re-weights the features
of different channels, identifying and emphasizing the feature channels most relevant to
the forecasting task while suppressing redundant information. The load forecasting result
is generated through the output layer. Spatial characteristics refer to the spatial distribution
patterns and relationships between load data from different locations or regions in power
grid load forecasting. Power grid loads typically vary across different geographical loca-
tions, and these differences may be related to factors such as the local climate, electricity
demand, population density, and industrial distribution. Capturing spatial characteristics
helps the model understand the dependencies and relationships between different regions,
leading to more accurate load predictions. Spatial characteristics are crucial in power grid
load forecasting because they reflect the interactions between nodes in the power system
and also reflect regional differences. If the model can effectively extract and utilize these
spatial features, it will have a better understanding of the load fluctuations and relation-
ships between different regions, improving the accuracy of predictions. For example, in
load forecasting, the load in some areas may be influenced by climate changes, while other
areas may be driven by industrial activities. Therefore, by modeling spatial characteristics,
the model can more comprehensively capture the load variation patterns in the power
grid, providing more reliable predictions in a dynamic and complex environment. The
innovation of this model lies in its effective integration of spatial feature extraction, time-
series modeling, and multiple attention mechanisms. It can capture both local and global
features and dynamically adjust the weights of temporal and channel features, significantly
improving the accuracy and stability of power grid load forecasting. Through multi-level
analysis and processing of complex load data, this model shows significant advantages in
terms of adaptability, generalization ability, and forecasting accuracy.

sections.title: 3.1 CNN Module
sections.text:
The main goal of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) is to extract significant
features from input data [16,17]. CNNs are primarily composed of convolutional layers
and pooling layers. Due to the local connectivity and weight-sharing characteristics of
convolutional layers, the key objective of CNNs is the automatic extraction of key features
and dimensionality reduction [39,40]. To enhance the depth of the model and improve the
ability to extract abstract features, the proposed model alternates between convolutional
and pooling layers in the CNN module, forming the feature extraction layer. Because
the fixed connection pattern of CNNs somewhat limits the number of feature extraction
layers, typically, 1 to 3 feature extraction layers are used in short-term load forecasting, with
the specific number of layers determined based on the model’s prediction performance.
Convolutional layers effectively extract complex dynamic features and local non-linear
features from historical load data using different convolutional kernels [41,42]. Meanwhile,
pooling layers reduce the data dimension through max pooling and average pooling
operations, preserving more meaningful information by compressing the extracted features.
Max pooling can extract the most significant local features from time-series data, such as
sharp fluctuations or sudden events in load variations over the short term. This helps
the model focus on key data changes at critical time points, thereby avoiding excessive
interference from noise. Meanwhile, average pooling smooths the time-series data by
pooling the average value within local time windows, helping the model capture the
overall trend and long-term patterns in the data, thereby reducing the impact of short-term
fluctuations on predictions. The combination of these pooling strategies allows the model
to retain important dynamic information while balancing noise and trends, improving
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 9 of 24
the feature extraction capability from time-series data and enhancing the accuracy and
robustness of load forecasting. This module employs the max pooling method, aiming to
retain more fluctuation information, thereby improving the model’s generalization ability.
However, CNNs are not effective at capturing the temporal dependencies in time-series
data. Therefore, to enhance the model’s performance, Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
techniques must be incorporated, combining CNN with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
networks. The combination of LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) with CNN is primarily
recommended due to the fact that CNN excels at extracting local features and patterns
from data, but it performs poorly in capturing the long-term dependencies and temporal
relationships in time-series data. CNN effectively extracts local dynamic features and non-
linear patterns from time-series data through convolutional operations, and in particular,
it excels at capturing short-term fluctuations and sudden events. However, power grid
load data typically exhibit long-term temporal dependencies, meaning that the current
load state is often influenced by the load history and trends from a previous period. In this
case, LSTM is well suited to handling such long-term dependencies. Through its gating
mechanisms, LSTM can retain past information and capture long-term patterns and trends
over extended periods. Therefore, combining CNN with LSTM allows the strengths of CNN
in local feature extraction to be integrated with LSTMs’ strengths in temporal modeling,
enabling the model to effectively capture both local features and long-term dependencies
in load data. This enhances the accuracy and robustness of power grid load forecasting.
Taking one feature extraction layer as an example, the preprocessed historical load
sequence is input into the CNN module, denoted as fin = [fin,1, · · ·, fin,t−1, fin,t, · · ·, fin,n].
The output vector of the CNN module can be represented as follows:
fout = S( fin × W1 + σ1), (1)
f p = M( fout ) +σ2, (2)
where fout is the output of the convolutional layer, f p is the output of the pooling layer, W
and σ are the weight matrix and bias vector, respectively, S is the activation function, ×
represents the convolution operation, and M(·) represents the max function.

sections.title: 3.2 LSTM Module
sections.text:
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks consist of three main gating mechanisms:
the forget gate, the input gate, and the output gate [ 30]. The forget gate determines
how much of the previous memory information and the new input information at the
current time step should be retained, using the sigmoid function. When the output of
this gate is 1, all information is retained, while a value of 0 causes all information to be
discarded. This gate design effectively addresses the common vanishing gradient problem
in Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), enabling the model to better capture long-term
dependencies. Through these gating mechanisms, LSTM can implement selective memory
between different time steps, retaining important historical information while discarding
irrelevant data, thus enhancing the model’s ability to handle sequential data. However,
LSTM may still lose some key information when processing very long input sequences. To
address this issue, CNN is used for preprocessing the input data, filtering out redundant
and irrelevant parts and thereby effectively improving the accuracy of load forecasting.

sections.title: 3.3 Multi-Head Self-Attention Model
sections.text:
Self-attention is a technique that allows the model to “pay attention” to the rela-
tionships between different parts of the input data. Intuitively, it acts like an intelligent
“highlighter” that can automatically identify and emphasize the most important parts of
the input data for the current task. For example, in power grid load forecasting, the load
data may include many time points and features, but not all time points or features are
equally important for the prediction. The self-attention mechanism calculates the relevance
between each part of the data and others, dynamically assigning different weights to each
part, allowing the model to focus more on the information that has a greater impact on
the prediction. This mechanism is especially suitable for handling long-sequence data or
complex non-linear relationships, as it can capture long-range dependencies in the data,
not just local or short-term patterns. In this way, self-attention helps the model better
understand the inherent structure of the data, thus improving prediction accuracy and
robustness. The Transformer model can efficiently handle long sequence data; as such, it
performs exceptionally well in tasks like grid load forecasting, which involve long-term de-
pendencies. The Transformer model employs the Self-Attention Mechanism, which allows
for parallel processing of the entire input sequence. This parallel computation capability
significantly improves the speed of model training and prediction, making it suitable for
processing large-scale grid data and meeting real-time requirements. Therefore, we use the
multi-head self-attention mechanism to enhance the model’s global modeling capability
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 11 of 24
and capture long-range dependencies between features. The multi-head self-attention
module is shown in Figure 3 and is represented as follows:
fout = BN (MHSA (LN ( fin))) +fin, (10)
where LN represents Layer Normalization, BN stands for Batch Normalization, and MHSA
stands for multi-head self-attention. The time series data first undergo layer normalization
(LN), then the data are reshaped into feature vectors. These feature vectors are used as the
original input features, which are further standardized through batch normalization and
then undergo a linear transformation to generate the query (Q), key (K), and value (V). To
further compress the temporal dimension and extract global information, the key (K) and
value (V) are first subjected to average pooling after generation. Subsequently, the query
(Q) along with the pooled key (K) and value (V) are fed into the multi-head self-attention
(MHSA) mechanism, which generates the attention output. The output of the self-attention
mechanism is then added to the original input features through a residual connection. This
approach not only preserves the original input information but also alleviates the vanishing
gradient problem, making the model easier to train.

sections.title: 3.4 Global Attention Model
sections.text:
The attention mechanism is a process that simulates how humans allocate attention
resources. Its core idea is to focus on key areas while diminishing attention to irrelevant
information, thereby enhancing the overall performance of the model. By filtering and
amplifying key features, it effectively filters out noise or unimportant information, signifi-
cantly improving the model’s ability to recognize important information and its prediction
accuracy. Unlike traditional methods that assign random weights, the attention mecha-
nism dynamically assigns weights to each input element using a probability distribution,
ensuring that the model focuses on the information that is most relevant to the task. This
mechanism not only addresses the potential information loss issue in LSTM when pro-
cessing very long sequences but also better preserves the global and local dependencies
in temporal features, thus optimizing the model’s expressive power and predictive per-
formance. Additionally, the attention mechanism is highly flexible and can be combined
with various neural network architectures, further enhancing the model’s adaptability and
generalization ability. Figure 4 visually illustrates the structure of this mechanism.

applied to the LSTM hidden layer output is denoted as αt, and the output of the LSTM

sections.title: 3.5 Channel Attention Model
sections.text:
In the global attention mechanism phase, the model captures the long-range temporal
dependencies of input features using the self-attention mechanism. This process helps
the model understand the temporal dynamics and trends of load data. However, while
the global attention mechanism effectively captures sequential information, it cannot
directly focus on the importance of each feature channel. Therefore, to further optimize
feature representation and enhance the model’s sensitivity to key predictive information
under the comprehensive modeling of both temporal and spatial features, we designed
a channel attention mechanism based on the SE (Squeeze-and-Excitation) module. This
mechanism applies weighted processing to the feature channels, automatically identifying
and reinforcing the channels most relevant to the task, while suppressing redundant and
Appl. Sci. 2025, 15, 2435 13 of 24
irrelevant channel features. The structure of the SE module is shown in Figure 1. Specifically,
the SE module first performs a “Squeeze” operation to compress the global information
of each channel, resulting in a channel-level description. Then, through the “Excitation”
operation, a weight coefficient is assigned to each channel, determining its contribution
to the final output. Finally, through the “Scale” operation, the channel weight coefficients
obtained in the “Excitation” step are applied to each channel of the original feature map,
adjusting the features of each channel accordingly. In detail, the channel weights obtained
after the “Excitation” step are element-wise-multiplied with the features of each channel in
the original feature map, thereby scaling the features of different channels. This process
highlights the channels that are most important for the task and suppresses those that are
less relevant. This ensures that the model can dynamically focus on the most predictive
channels while suppressing redundant or irrelevant information, thereby improving the
model’s performance in tasks like grid load forecasting. The specific operations of Squeeze,
Excitation, and Scale are as follows:
The Squeeze operation compresses each feature channel into a real number, called a
descriptor, by applying global pooling to the input features. This descriptor represents the
statistical information of the corresponding channel, which is typically achieved through
global average pooling. The unweighted feature map U is summarized and averaged,
resulting in a multi-dimensional statistic z ∈ RC. The n-th element of z is calculated as

representing the channel weights of the feature map U. The final output of the SE module
is achieved through the scaling operation, where the weight vector s and the unweighted
input feature map U are element-wise-multiplied by the weight of each channel. The
output of the n-th channel is calculated as follows:
ˆun = Fscale (un, sn) =snun, (16)
where ˆun ∈ ˆU = [ˆu1, ˆu2, · · ·, ˆuC], ˆU is the final overall output, and sn is the weight of the
n-th channel.

sections.title: 4 Case Study
sections.text:
This section validates the effectiveness of the CNN-MHSA-LSTM-GAM-CAM hybrid
model on a real distributed network load dataset through comprehensive comparative
experiments. In addition, the effects of each attention module are analyzed, revealing the
potential of the attention mechanism in short-term load forecasting.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Data and Evaluation Metrics
sections.text:
This study deeply analyzes the effectiveness and performance of power load forecast-
ing models by exploring several representative datasets. Each dataset provides a unique
perspective and basis for validation, helping to comprehensively understand the complexi-
ties faced when forecasting electricity demand. These datasets vary in scope and geographic
background, allowing the study to cover the characteristics of power load variations in
different environments, further enhancing the adaptability and generalization ability of the
forecasting model. Specifically, the study uses three main datasets: the Panama Case Study
Dataset [43], the Daily Electricity Price and Demand Dataset (Victoria, Australia) [44], and
the Household Electric Power Consumption Dataset [45]. All these datasets are publicly
available and come from multiple authoritative sources, providing a solid data foundation
for model validation and cross-regional comparisons. Through an in-depth analysis of these
datasets, this study aims to provide more comprehensive and multidimensional research
results in the field of power load forecasting. The dataset descriptions are as follows:
The Panama Case Study Dataset: This dataset contains integrated information from
multiple data sources with high data quality and rich features. The time span of the dataset
is from 2015 to 2020, providing several years of historical power load data. The data
granularity is recorded on an hourly basis, ensuring detail and precision. The dataset
has been preprocessed, and all data sources have been merged into a CSV file indexed
by date and time. Additionally, there are CSV files for load forecasting and two Excel
files containing recommended regression variables and 14 training/testing dataset pairs.
The data quality is high, though there may be some sparsity due to manual input for
certain data, such as during holidays and school periods. Overall, this dataset offers
comprehensive and detailed information for power load forecasting and is suitable for
training and testing machine learning and forecasting algorithms. The forecasting time
span is weekly, specifically starting from Saturday and ending on the next Friday. A 72 h
unseen data gap must be considered during prediction, meaning that when predicting next
week’s load, only data recorded up to the last hour on Tuesday are used. The load data is
recorded hourly, which helps capture short-term fluctuations and variations in power load,
thus improving prediction accuracy.
The Daily Electricity Price and Demand Dataset: This dataset covers 2016 days of
data from 1 January 2015 to 6 October 2020, recording daily electricity demand and related
variables in the state of Victoria, Australia. The data granularity is daily, and the dataset is
of high quality, covering various aspects such as electricity demand, price, weather, and
calendar information, providing comprehensive features for power demand forecasting.
The dataset includes negative RRP (Regional Reference Price) data, reflecting the special
market conditions during the pandemic, which adds to the dataset’s diversity and research
value. Overall, this dataset provides rich and detailed information for electricity demand
forecasting and related research. The forecasting time span is from 1 January 2015 to 6
October 2020, totaling 2016 days. The load data are recorded daily, with each data point
representing the total electricity demand of the day (in MWh). This daily granularity is
suitable for medium- to long-term power demand forecasting and analysis, capturing
seasonal changes and long-term trends in electricity demand.
The Household Electric Power Consumption Dataset: This dataset records electricity
consumption data for a household from December 2006 to November 2010, with a total of
2,075,259 measurement records. The data granularity is per minute, providing electricity
consumption information for each minute. Approximately 1.25% of the measurements
are missing, and missing values are represented by consecutive semicolons. Despite the
small amount of missing data, all timestamps are fully recorded, ensuring high data quality.
This dataset provides rich information for fine-grained analysis of electricity consumption,
